From Prototype to Commercial Reality
This regulatory shift transforms what was previously a compliance cost into a potential revenue opportunity through Seabound’s unique waste-to-resource approach.

Seabound’s technology uses calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) to absorb CO₂ from ship exhaust, converting it into limestone that’s stored onboard until the vessel returns to port. This calcium looping approach offers several advantages over traditional carbon capture systems that produce liquefied CO₂, and represents the first commercial application of this technology in marine environments.

“Shipping cement is emissions-intensive, and Seabound’s system gives us a clear path to reduce those Scope 3 emissions while enhancing our circular use of captured CO₂,” said Lars Erik Marcussen, Project Manager, Logistics at Heidelberg Materials Northern Europe.

This regulatory shift transforms what was previously a compliance cost into a potential revenue opportunity through Seabound’s unique waste-to-resource approach.

The containerized design allows for easy installation with minimal vessel modification and suits all vessel types. The modular system offers flexibility, shipowners can start with one module to meet basic regulatory requirements and scale up as thresholds increase or customer demands grow.

For shipowners considering the technology, Seabound has designed with operational simplicity in mind. The system requires no crew training, uses non-toxic materials, and operates with full automation. The current lead time is six to nine months, which the company aims to accelerate significantly.

“The upfront capex is very low, really trying to lower the barrier to entry,” Fredriksson notes. “Unlike something like ammonia, we don’t need to take the same extent of safety precautions. It’s not as complicated when you’re dealing with a simpler technology like this.”
